back: Training FLOPs $\approx6ND$: about $2N$ forward and $4N$ backward per token, times $D$ tokens. A first-order estimate for dense transformers.

front: Parameters of one GPT-2-style block (width d, MLP 4d)

back: 124,439,808 with a tied output head; 163,037,184 with a separate head ($V=50257$, $d=768$, $L=12$, ctx 1024).
$L(N,D)=A/N^\alpha+B/D^\beta+E$; $E$ is the irreducible loss of the text.

front: Why is 20 tokens/parameter only a rule of thumb?
back: The loss is flat near the optimum, the fitted constants are uncertain (with the quoted constants the grid minimum is at a higher ratio, yet only about 0.007 nats better), and deployment cost favours smaller, longer-trained models.
Training cost is paid once, inference cost forever; a smaller model trained on many more tokens is cheaper to serve at similar quality.
Concatenate documents with end-of-text separators and cut the stream into blocks; $x$ = block, $y$ = block shifted by one. Wastes no padding.

front: Why split by document before packing?
back: To avoid the same document (or near-copies) appearing in both train and validation, which makes validation loss optimistic.
$|S_n(A)\cap S_n(B)|/|S_n(A)\cup S_n(B)|$ over sets of word n-gram shingles.
Short hash signatures whose agreement probability equals Jaccard similarity; bucketing signatures finds candidate near-duplicates without comparing all pairs.
Duplicates waste compute and cause memorisation (verbatim regurgitation); it is among the most effective cleaning steps.

front: Training memory per parameter (fp32 Adam, no activations)

back: $2\cdot L\cdot d\cdot T$ numbers per sequence (keys and values for every layer and token); grows linearly with context and batch.

front: Expected loss at step 0 and what else to watch
back: About $\ln V$ (near uniform). Then watch the train/validation gap (overfitting), spikes (learning rate, bad batches) and plateaus (under-training, noisy data).
